questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which selective medium is used to isolate Neisseria gonorrhoeae from genital specimens?
options: Thayer-Martin medium with vancomycin, colistin and nystatin
Thiosulphate citrate bile salt sucrose agar
questions.concept: The antibiotic supplement suppresses commensal flora while the chocolate agar base and carbon dioxide atmosphere support this fastidious oxidase-positive Gram-negative diplococcus.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which capsular serogroups of Neisseria meningitidis are covered by the quadrivalent conjugate vaccine?
questions.concept: Group B polysaccharide resembles human neural tissue so it is poorly immunogenic and required a separate protein-based vaccine, which is why it is absent from the quadrivalent conjugate product.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which organism requires both factor X and factor V for growth and shows satellitism around Staphylococcus aureus on blood agar?
questions.concept: Haemin and NAD are released by staphylococcal haemolysis, so colonies grow only near the streak; chocolate agar supplies both factors directly, which is why it is the routine medium.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which Haemophilus influenzae serotype caused most invasive childhood disease before vaccination, and what is the capsular polysaccharide?
options: Type b, with a polyribosyl ribitol phosphate capsule
Type a, with a galactose capsule
Type f, with a glucose capsule
questions.concept: Conjugating the polyribosyl ribitol phosphate capsule to a protein carrier made it immunogenic in infants and nearly eliminated invasive type b disease, leaving non-typeable strains as the main cause of otitis and exacerbations.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which medium is used for the primary isolation of Bordetella pertussis, and why is it potato-based with charcoal or blood?
options: Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe medium, because charcoal and blood absorb inhibitory fatty acids
MacConkey agar, because of lactose fermentation
questions.concept: The organism is extremely fastidious and sensitive to fatty acids and peroxides, and the mercury-drop colonies appear only after several days, so PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab is now the preferred test.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which toxin of Bordetella pertussis causes lymphocytosis and blocks Gi-mediated signalling by ADP-ribosylation?
questions.concept: Inhibiting Gi leaves adenylate cyclase disinhibited and impairs chemotaxis, while tracheal cytotoxin destroys ciliated cells, producing the paroxysmal cough that persists after the organism has been cleared.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Brucellosis is best diagnosed serologically by which test, and why must the prozone phenomenon be considered?
options: Standard tube agglutination test, because very high antibody can give a false negative at low dilutions
questions.concept: Testing must extend to high dilutions to avoid missing a positive; blood culture on biphasic Castaneda medium held for several weeks remains the definitive test.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why does Neisseria gonorrhoeae not confer lasting immunity after infection, allowing repeated episodes?
options: Antigenic variation of pili and Opa proteins with no protective capsular immunity
It is intracellular and hidden from antibody
It produces an IgA protease that eliminates all antibody
questions.concept: Continuous pilin gene rearrangement means each infection presents new epitopes, which is also the principal obstacle to a gonococcal vaccine, unlike the meningococcus where capsular immunity is protective.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Neisseria and Haemophilus

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which intracytoplasmic inclusion is pathognomonic of rabies and where is it best sought?
options: Negri bodies in hippocampal and cerebellar Purkinje neurons
Cowdry type A bodies in the cortex
questions.concept: Negri bodies are present in about 70 percent of cases, so their absence does not exclude rabies, and the direct fluorescent antibody test on brain tissue is the reference standard.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which category of animal exposure requires both rabies vaccine and immunoglobulin?
options: Category III, with transdermal bites, scratches with bleeding or mucosal contamination with saliva
Category I, touching or feeding an animal
Category II, minor scratches without bleeding
Any contact with a vaccinated dog
questions.concept: Immunoglobulin is infiltrated into and around the wound to neutralise virus locally before vaccine-induced antibody appears, and thorough washing with soap and water for 15 minutes is the essential first step.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which polio vaccine can cause vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis and circulating vaccine-derived virus?
questions.concept: The attenuated strains can revert to neurovirulence, especially type 2, which is why type 2 was withdrawn from the oral vaccine and inactivated vaccine has been introduced into routine schedules.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why does the inactivated polio vaccine provide less intestinal mucosal immunity than the oral vaccine?
options: It induces systemic IgG but little secretory IgA in the gut, so it does not interrupt faecal transmission as effectively
It is given at a later age
questions.concept: This difference explains why oral vaccine was preferred for outbreak control and eradication campaigns, while inactivated vaccine reliably prevents paralysis in the vaccinated individual.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which enterovirus is the commonest cause of hand, foot and mouth disease, and which is associated with severe neurological complications in outbreaks?
options: Coxsackievirus A16 commonly, with enterovirus 71 causing brainstem encephalitis
questions.concept: Enterovirus 71 outbreaks in the Asia-Pacific region have caused fatal brainstem encephalitis and pulmonary oedema, which is why surveillance distinguishes it from the milder coxsackie A16 disease.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which clinical syndrome is characteristic of coxsackie B virus and presents with fever and severe pleuritic chest or abdominal pain?
questions.concept: Coxsackie B also causes myocarditis and pericarditis, whereas herpangina with posterior oral vesicles is typical of coxsackie A, and both groups cause aseptic meningitis.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: In the pathogenesis of rabies, why is post-exposure prophylaxis effective even after the bite?
options: The virus replicates locally in muscle for days to weeks before entering peripheral nerves
Antibody can neutralise virus within neurons
The vaccine eliminates the virus from the brain
questions.concept: The long and variable incubation period reflects this local phase and the distance to the central nervous system, so proximal head and neck bites have shorter incubation and greater urgency.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why is the intradermal rabies vaccine regimen used in India, and what is its principal advantage?
options: It uses one-fifth of the intramuscular dose at multiple sites, giving equivalent immunogenicity at lower cost
It avoids the need for immunoglobulin
It gives lifelong immunity in one dose
It can be given after symptoms appear
questions.concept: Dose sparing greatly extends limited vaccine supplies in high-burden settings, but it demands trained staff and correct technique, and it does not remove the need for immunoglobulin in category III exposure.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rhabdoviruses and Picornaviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Which influenza surface protein is the target of oseltamivir?
questions.concept: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid to release progeny virions, so its inhibition traps virus at the cell surface; the M2 channel is the target of the older and now largely useless amantadine.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Antigenic shift in influenza A refers to:
options: Reassortment of gene segments producing a new subtype with pandemic potential
questions.concept: Because the genome is segmented, coinfection of an intermediate host such as the pig allows whole-segment exchange, generating a haemagglutinin to which the population has no immunity.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Which complication of mumps is the commonest cause of acquired unilateral sensorineural deafness in children?
questions.concept: Orchitis and aseptic meningitis are commoner overall, but the abrupt permanent hearing loss from labyrinthine involvement is the classic long-term sequela, and vaccination has largely removed it.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Which measles complication appears years after infection and presents with progressive myoclonus and dementia?
questions.concept: Defective viral matrix protein permits persistent infection of neurons, and the electroencephalogram shows periodic high-amplitude complexes with very high antibody titre in cerebrospinal fluid; it is uniformly fatal.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Why is the measles vaccine given at 9 months in India but at 12 to 15 months in many high-income countries?
options: Higher force of infection means earlier exposure, so protection is needed before maternal antibody has fully waned
The vaccine is more potent in India
Higher risk of febrile seizures later
questions.concept: Giving it earlier accepts slightly lower seroconversion in exchange for protecting infants during the period of highest mortality, and a second dose at 16 to 24 months covers primary vaccine failure.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Which specimen and test are preferred for laboratory confirmation of SARS-CoV-2 in the first week of illness?
options: Nasopharyngeal swab for real-time reverse transcription PCR
questions.concept: Antibody appears only after the first week and reflects past infection, so molecular detection of viral RNA from the upper respiratory tract is the diagnostic test during acute illness.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Congenital rubella syndrome risk is highest when maternal infection occurs:
questions.concept: Organogenesis determines the pattern of cataract, deafness and cardiac defect, and infection after 20 weeks rarely causes structural damage, which is why gestational age determines counselling.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.topic: Respiratory viruses: influenza, SARS-CoV-2, measles, mumps, rubella
questions.stem: Why does an influenza vaccine need annual reformulation, unlike the measles vaccine?
options: Continuous antigenic drift in haemagglutinin and neuraminidase erodes strain-specific immunity
Influenza vaccine is inactivated and short-lived
questions.concept: Error-prone polymerase and immune selection drive drift each season, whereas measles is antigenically stable with a single serotype, which is precisely why it is theoretically eradicable.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Orthomyxoviruses and Paramyxoviruses

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which feature of Mycoplasma explains its resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics?
options: It lacks a cell wall and has sterols in its membrane
questions.concept: With no peptidoglycan there is no target for beta-lactams, so macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are used, and the organism requires cholesterol-enriched media forming fried-egg colonies.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which Chlamydia trachomatis serovars cause lymphogranuloma venereum?
questions.concept: Serovars A to C cause trachoma and D to K cause genital infection and inclusion conjunctivitis, whereas the L serovars are more invasive and target lymphatic tissue, producing buboes and the groove sign.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which stain demonstrates the intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies of Chlamydia trachomatis in conjunctival scrapings?
questions.concept: Iodine staining of glycogen-containing inclusions and direct immunofluorescence are alternatives, but nucleic acid amplification has become the test of choice for both ocular and genital disease.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which characteristic of the chlamydial developmental cycle explains why treatment must be prolonged?
options: The metabolically inactive extracellular elementary body is not susceptible, and only the intracellular reticulate body replicates
questions.concept: Only the replicating form is drug-susceptible, so a single dose of azithromycin works because of the drug's long intracellular half-life, and shorter-acting agents need a week or more.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is associated with which extrapulmonary complication mediated by cold agglutinins?
questions.concept: IgM cold agglutinins against the erythrocyte I antigen arise from cross-reactivity, and other extrapulmonary features include erythema multiforme, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which rickettsial disease is transmitted by the human body louse and is associated with war and famine, with recrudescence as Brill-Zinsser disease?
options: Epidemic typhus due to Rickettsia prowazekii
Endemic typhus due to Rickettsia typhi
Scrub typhus due to Orientia tsutsugamushi
questions.concept: The organism persists in lymphoid tissue for years, so recrudescence can seed a new louse-borne outbreak, which is why delousing is central to control.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which reproductive complication of untreated chlamydial cervicitis makes screening of young sexually active women worthwhile?
options: Tubal factor infertility and ectopic pregnancy from silent salpingitis
questions.concept: Because up to 70 percent of infections are asymptomatic, damage accumulates silently, and opportunistic screening with nucleic acid amplification on a self-taken vulvovaginal swab detects it.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why is doxycycline effective against Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma despite their very different cell structures?
options: All three are susceptible because tetracyclines penetrate cells and inhibit the 30S ribosome, a target common to all bacteria
All three lack a cell wall
All three are obligate intracellular organisms
questions.concept: Intracellular penetration plus a conserved ribosomal target explains the breadth, which is why doxycycline is the empirical choice for atypical pneumonia and for undifferentiated fever in rickettsial endemic areas.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Rickettsia, Chlamydia and Mycoplasma

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Blood for culture in suspected bacteraemia should ideally be collected:
options: As two or three sets from separate venepuncture sites before antibiotics, with adequate volume
As a single sample from an indwelling line
questions.concept: Volume is the single most important determinant of yield, and separate sets distinguish true bacteraemia from skin contamination; timing to fever spikes adds little because bacteraemia is usually continuous or intermittent.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which transport medium is used for stool specimens when culture will be delayed?
questions.concept: Cary-Blair preserves enteric pathogens including Vibrio, Salmonella and Shigella, whereas Stuart and Amies suit swabs of other sites and alkaline peptone water is an enrichment rather than a transport medium.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which specimen is preferred for the diagnosis of typhoid fever in the first week of illness?
questions.concept: Bacteraemia is present from the outset, whereas stool and urine become positive in the second and third weeks; bone marrow culture has the highest yield overall and remains positive after antibiotics.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which molecular method allows quantification of a pathogen's nucleic acid in real time and is used for HIV and hepatitis viral loads?
options: Real-time quantitative PCR with fluorescent probes
questions.concept: Signal accumulation is measured cycle by cycle, so the threshold cycle relates directly to starting template amount, which permits monitoring of treatment response and detection of virological failure.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why must a paired serum sample be used when a single antibody titre is being interpreted in an endemic area?
options: A fourfold rise between acute and convalescent samples demonstrates recent infection against a high background seroprevalence
A single sample cannot be diluted
IgM is undetectable in acute illness
questions.concept: In areas of high prior exposure a single raised titre may reflect past infection or vaccination, so demonstrating a rise, or detecting IgM, is what establishes recency.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which technique identifies bacteria and fungi directly from a colony within minutes by protein fingerprinting?
questions.concept: Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionisation time-of-flight compares ribosomal protein spectra with a database, shortening identification from days to minutes, though susceptibility testing still requires separate methods.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which sample is most appropriate for diagnosing tuberculous meningitis by molecular testing?
options: Cerebrospinal fluid, sent in adequate volume for a cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test
questions.concept: Sensitivity depends heavily on volume because the disease is paucibacillary, and the ultra version of the cartridge assay was developed specifically to improve detection in cerebrospinal fluid.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why is a nucleic acid amplification test unsuitable as a test of cure immediately after treating gonorrhoea or chlamydia?
options: Residual nucleic acid from non-viable organisms can remain detectable for weeks, giving a false positive
The test loses sensitivity after treatment
questions.concept: For this reason a test of cure, when indicated, is deferred for several weeks, and culture is preferred where confirmation of viability and susceptibility testing are needed.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Diagnostic Microbiology

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which test remains reactive for life after treated syphilis and therefore cannot be used to monitor treatment?
options: Treponemal specific tests such as TPHA or FTA-ABS
questions.concept: Non-treponemal tests measuring anticardiolipin antibody fall with successful treatment and are used to monitor response, whereas specific antitreponemal antibody persists indefinitely.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which condition causes a biological false-positive VDRL?
options: Systemic lupus erythematosus and antiphospholipid syndrome
questions.concept: Because the test detects antibody to cardiolipin rather than to the organism, autoimmune disease, pregnancy, malaria and some viral infections can give false positives, which is why a specific treponemal test is used to confirm.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which spirochaete is transmitted through skin abraded by contact with water contaminated by rodent urine?
questions.concept: Occupational and recreational water exposure explains outbreaks after flooding, and the organism is best seen by dark ground microscopy or cultured in Ellinghausen-McCullough-Johnson-Harris medium.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which stage of syphilis is most infectious, and why?
options: Secondary syphilis, because moist mucocutaneous lesions teem with treponemes
questions.concept: Condylomata lata and mucous patches are highly infectious, whereas tertiary lesions contain few organisms and represent a hypersensitivity response rather than active proliferation.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which relapsing fever spirochaete is louse-borne and shows antigenic variation explaining the recurrent fever pattern?
questions.concept: Sequential expression of variable major proteins allows the organism to escape antibody, producing successive febrile episodes as each new antigenic variant proliferates before being cleared.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which serological test is the reference standard for leptospirosis and requires paired sera?
options: Microscopic agglutination test using live serovars
questions.concept: It is technically demanding and available only in reference laboratories, so IgM ELISA or rapid tests are used in the field, with culture of blood in the first week and urine thereafter.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which clinical stage of Lyme disease is characterised by erythema migrans, and what is the vector?
options: Early localised disease, transmitted by Ixodes ticks
Early disseminated disease, transmitted by sandflies
questions.concept: The expanding annular lesion with central clearing appears days to weeks after the bite, and early doxycycline prevents the later carditis, neuroborreliosis and arthritis.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why can Treponema pallidum not be grown in artificial culture, and how does this shape diagnosis?
options: It is a microaerophilic obligate parasite with limited biosynthetic capacity, so diagnosis relies on microscopy, serology and molecular tests
It forms spores that resist culture
questions.concept: Its reduced genome lacks many biosynthetic pathways, so it is propagated only in rabbit testis, and this is why dark ground microscopy of a moist lesion plus paired serology remains the diagnostic mainstay.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Spirochaetes

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which biological indicator is used to validate autoclave performance?
questions.concept: These spores require moist heat at 121 degrees to be killed, whereas Bacillus atrophaeus spores are used for hot air oven and ethylene oxide validation, so matching indicator to process matters.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which method is used to sterilise heat-labile items such as flexible endoscopes and plastic implants?
options: Ethylene oxide gas or low-temperature hydrogen peroxide plasma
questions.concept: Ethylene oxide is a highly penetrating alkylating agent but is toxic and needs prolonged aeration, and plasma or peracetic acid systems have shorter cycles for the same class of items.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which process removes microorganisms from a heat-labile solution such as serum without heat?
options: Membrane filtration through a 0.22 micrometre filter
questions.concept: Filtration excludes bacteria and fungi but not viruses or mycoplasma, which is why filtered biological products are still tested for viral contamination.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which level of disinfection is required for an instrument that contacts mucous membranes but does not penetrate tissue, such as a laryngoscope blade?
questions.concept: Under the Spaulding classification, critical items entering sterile tissue require sterilisation, semi-critical items contacting mucosa require high-level disinfection, and non-critical items touching intact skin need only low-level disinfection.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which chemical agent is a high-level disinfectant that is not inactivated by organic material and is widely used for endoscopes?
questions.concept: It is sporicidal with prolonged contact and non-corrosive, though it is irritant and sensitising to staff, which is why ortho-phthalaldehyde and peracetic acid have gained ground.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which principle explains why moist heat sterilises at a lower temperature than dry heat?
options: Steam denatures and coagulates proteins and delivers latent heat of condensation, whereas dry heat kills by oxidation
Moist heat penetrates spores through pores
Dry heat cannot kill spores at all
questions.concept: Because coagulation needs less energy than oxidation, 121 degrees for 15 minutes suffices with steam whereas the hot air oven needs 160 degrees for 2 hours.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which medium is described as an enriched medium rather than an enrichment medium?
questions.concept: An enriched solid medium has nutrients added to support fastidious organisms, whereas an enrichment liquid medium selectively encourages one organism while inhibiting others, a distinction frequently confused.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why is Tyndallisation used for media containing sugars or gelatin?
options: Intermittent heating at 100 degrees on successive days kills spores as they germinate between cycles, without the caramelisation caused by autoclaving
questions.concept: Discontinuous sterilisation exploits the vulnerability of germinating spores, and inspissation at lower temperature serves the same purpose for egg-based media such as Lowenstein-Jensen.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Why does a Bowie-Dick test complement a chemical and biological indicator in autoclave monitoring?
options: It detects air removal and steam penetration failure in a porous load, which the other indicators may miss
It tests for residual ethylene oxide
questions.concept: Trapped air prevents steam from reaching the load even when the recorded temperature is correct, so the three approaches together cover physical, chemical and biological assurance.
questions.reference: Ananthanarayan and Paniker's Textbook of Microbiology 11e, Ch. Sterilisation and Disinfection
